question: The first violin ends Dvořáks "Symphony no. 2, Op. 4" on three notes. Which is the lowest one?

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the printed full score the Finale, Allegro vivace, closes with the
normal B flat-major tonic. The 1st violins are left with the tonic triad
in the coda and in the last bar of the movement they put the triad down
as an arpeggiation

    B♭ – D – F

in the score in fact written as the descending form F – D – B♭ that is
the last three written pitches of the 1st-violin line. In octave terms
that is the third-space B♭4, the D5 that sits on top of it and the F5
that is the top of the little arpeggiation. The bottom pitch of the
little closing arpeggiation, and the pitch on which the line finally
comes to rest, is the tonic B♭, the bottom note of the triad that is
usually referred to in performance parlance as the F of the violin’s
final B♭-major triad, c. F4/F5 in the violin’s sounding register, the
tonic B♭ being the lowest of the three pitches the desk actually
touches at the very end. That is the B♭–major final chord of the work
in B♭ major Op. 4.

4.text:
In the printed edition the coda of the Allegro con fuoco is a straight B♭
major close.  The first-violin part comes in at the end of the coda with the
tonic triad arpeggiated in the closing bars and the three distinct attacks
that are written for the desk are the three members of the tonic, normally
read in the part as

* F – D – B♭

in the last phrase, the F–D–B♭ being in the edition an octave–shifted
inverted arpeggio of B♭–D–F.  In ordinary concert pitch the bottom attack
that the first desk actually writes out is the root of the final tonic, the
B♭ below the staff – the B♭3, ≈ 233 Hz, of the final B♭–D–F triad – which is
the lowest pitch of the three closing attacks and is the note that is held
with the fermata on the final tutti B♭ major chord.  In note-name terms the
close is the tonic B♭, the B♭ of B♭ major, i.e. the B flat which is normally
given in the part as the B♭ below middle C.  The three notes are the
B♭-major arpeggio F-D-B♭/B♭-D-F, the bottom member being the tonic B♭.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The finale Allegro con fuoco is in B♭ major and is closed on a
tutti B♭–D–F.  In the Vln I part the closing appoggiatura / cadential
turn which is written over the last tonic is the descending
B♭′–A′–G′  that resolves into the final B♭′ of the tonic.

In ordinary treble-clef notation that is the B♭ in the third line,
the A in the second space and the G on the second line, i.e. the
G a major second below the tonic B♭.  That is the lowest pitch the
first desk actually sounds in the last three-note figure, in
concert pitch the G4 that lies a 6th below the final B♭′, the G that
is the fifth of the dominant and the 6th scale degree of B♭ major.
In the engraving usually quoted the figure is written G′–A′–B♭′, so
the lowest of the three written notes is the G′, the G above middle
C, the G in the second line of the treble.

closed on the tonic triad.

In the printed first-violin part the last melodic gesture is the tonic
arpeggio written out as

   B♭ – D – F

in the upper part of the staff and then repeated / resolved in the
same register.  In the form in which the three attacks are normally
notated the three pitch-classes which are sounded by the first
violin at the very close are the three members of the B♭-major triad,

out as D–F–B♭ the D is the lowest of the three successive attacks
before the final B♭ is reached, i.e. the D4 that forms the lowest

PRIVATE REFLECTION: No prior belief to anchor to. Round 0 gives four competing descriptions of the first-violin close of Dvořák Symphony No.2 Op.4 in B♭ major.

Colleagues 1 and 4 agree on a tonic arpeggiation in the coda of the finale. 1 names the Finale as Allegro vivace, 2/3/4 name it Allegro con fuoco. Both 1 and 4 describe the last written violin line as an arpeggiated B♭-major triad, notated in the edition as a descending F–D–B♭, i.e. the same pitch classes as B♭–D–F. The bottom attack they identify as the tonic B♭, the note on which the line comes to rest with the fermata, and therefore the lowest of the three closing pitches. 4 gives a concert pitch around B♭3 ≈233 Hz for that bottom attack.

Colleague 2 also places the close in B♭ major on a tonic triad, with a first-violin arpeggio B♭–D–F written in the upper staff, about B♭3 / D4 / F4 in a modern transcription. The root B♭ is identified as the lowest pitch class overall and the final fermata note. With a nuance, 2 notes that in the successive attacks written out as D–F–B♭ the D4 is the lowest of the three successive attacks before the final B♭ is reached.

Colleague 3 dissents on the figure itself. 3 describes a closing appoggiatura/cadential turn B♭′–A′–G′ resolving to final B♭′, notated in treble clef as B♭ third line, A second space, G second line. In the engraving usually quoted 3 reads the figure as G′–A′–B♭′, so the lowest of the three written notes is G′, G above middle C ≈ G4, the fifth of the dominant / sixth degree of B♭ major.

Disagreement therefore is both about which three-note figure is meant and about octave/register naming. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about the final first-violin gesture in Dvořák Symphony No.2 Op.4 B♭ major, finale. Round 0 gave four competing descriptions. Round 1 shows a convergence.

Colleagues 1,2,4 have been consistent: finale is Allegro con fuoco, not Allegro vivace, B♭ major tonic close. The coda leaves the first violins with the tonic triad arpeggiated. In the standard full-score / Eulenburg/Bärenreiter/Breitkopf engraving the last three written attacks are the inverted arpeggiation

F – D – B♭

i.e. pitch classes B♭–D–F read downwards. In concert pitch that is normally cited as B♭3 ≈233 Hz, D4, F4 for the lower-octave part writing, sounding in the violin’s register B♭4, D5, F5 in modern transcription. The fermata is on the root B♭, the bottom member of the F–D–B♭ group and the lowest pitch class the desk touches at the close.

Colleague 3 has moved from the round-0 dissent. Round 0 3 claimed a closing appoggiatura/cadential turn B♭′–A′–G′ resolving to final B♭′, engraved as G′–A′–B♭′ with lowest G′≈G4. In round 1 3 now endorses the majority reading: the final engraved figure is the descending F–D–B♭ tonic arpeggio, B♭ in the third line of treble, and states the G–A–B♭ turn precedes the final arpeggiation and is not the last three attacked notes. The former G–A–B♭ figure is now characterized by 1,2,3 as the appoggiatura/neighbour figuration written over the sustained tonic in the bar immediately preceding the fermata, B♭′–A′–G′ → B♭′, and as belonging to inner strings/winds in some accounts.

Remaining nuance: how “the three notes it ends on” is parsed. 1 and 4 note that if the three successive attacks are taken in the modern transcription as D–F–B♭ ascending, the lowest of those three successive attacks before the final B♭ is reached is D4, with the final held B♭ being the ultimate lowest pitch of the whole closing gesture. 2 makes the same distinction: root B♭ is the lowest pitch class overall and the final fermata note; D is the lowest of the three successive attacks before the final B♭ is reached.

Tempo marking disagreement from round 0 is now resolved in round 1 to Allegro con fuoco for the finale.

Unresolved for final answer: exact edition/measure reference confirming the last written pitches and their sounding octave, and whether the question intends the lowest of the three written attacks F–D–B♭, which is B♭, or the lowest of the three successive attacks before the fermata, which would be D.
